The former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock has been appointed by the Australian cabinet to review whether current laws sufficiently protect the human right to religious freedom. This appointment aims to prevent a contentious debate over religious amendments in a same-sex marriage bill. Treasurer Scott Morrison emphasized that this review is not a replacement for those specific amendments.

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull highlighted the importance of carefully examining religious freedom in the context of the recent yes vote and upcoming legislation on marriage equality. While some senior conservatives, such as Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann, have suggested that a religious freedom bill could be addressed separately next year, others including Morrison and senator David Fawcett argue it should be considered alongside the marriage bill.

Ruddock has been tasked with completing his report by 31 March. Turnbull pointed out that various legislative proposals to protect religious freedom have been suggested recently, though many extend beyond the immediate marriage equality issue. He cautioned parliament to be careful in considering these broader proposals.

The Prime Minister warned of the risks of unintended consequences when legislating protections for fundamental rights, including religious freedom. He expressed concern over broadly worded bill of rights-style laws that might create legal uncertainties. The review is intended as a timely expert assessment to guide any necessary legislative changes.

Turnbull affirmed that Ruddock is well-suited to lead the review, citing his experience as Australia’s special envoy for human rights. The government seeks to ensure that any reforms to protect religious freedom are thoughtfully developed and appropriately targeted.
